games.explanation: Sanchez has been quietly excellent all year, but the split nobody wants to talk about is how much more mortal he looks against right-handed bats, and the Mets happen to run a lineup full of them. Lindor, Bichette, and Vientos have all done real damage to righties this season, and Soto is Soto regardless of which arm slot is throwing. Tong is the obvious concern, but two coin-flip teams separated by four Elo points shouldn't be priced anywhere near this far apart. At +146 on a game the market itself projects within a run, you're getting paid to take the side with the better bats.

Wacha is the kind of soft-contact righty who looks fine in the box score until a lineup full of left-handed thump gets three cracks at him, and Pittsburgh happens to bring exactly that. Lowe, Reynolds, and Cruz have all posted xwOBAs north of .330 against right-handed pitching, and Wacha's barrel rate against righties has quietly climbed to 9.1%, which is where good swings turn into damage. Bachar walks too many hitters to love, but the whiffs are real and Kansas City's lineup outside of Witt does not exactly punish mistakes. Getting the better team at plus money in a game the market has priced as a coin flip is the entire argument, and +102 is a gift.

Hunter Brown is quietly having an ace-caliber year, which is exactly why a plus-money price on the team facing him feels wrong until you look at who's stepping in the box. Acuña has been the best hitter on either roster against right-handed pitching, and Olson and Baldwin round out a top four that punishes anyone who nibbles, which Brown does more than his reputation suggests. Perez is the obvious hole in the ticket, but a projected one-run game at plus money doesn't require him to be good, just competent enough to hand it off. Getting +126 on the better team by a comfortable Elo margin is the pitch, and the lineup is the reason it cashes.

The market keeps treating Washington like a rebuild team getting bullied on the road, and it hasn't caught up to the fact that the Cardinals are the ones with the deeper problems tonight. St. Louis is a full 89 Elo points behind the Nats here, which is quietly one of the bigger gaps you'll find on a plus-money dog all week. Wood at the top of the order is the kind of left-handed bat that turns a coin-flip game into a game the underdog wins outright, and Irvin's mediocrity is already baked into the price. Getting +126 on the better team is the kind of math the book usually hides better than this.

Brock Stewart's overall line looks like a buzzsaw until you notice lefties have been teeing off on him all year, and the Giants happen to run a left-handed heavy order through the top of the card. Jung Hoo Lee is exactly the profile that makes this arm uncomfortable, and the split gap is enormous: righties are hitting Stewart like a Cy Young winner while lefties own a .326 xwOBA against him. Project a one-run game where the board has priced a Dodgers walkover, and the number stops making sense. +229 on a coin flip dressed up as a longshot is the entire pitch.

Sandy Alcantara's name still moves lines like it's 2022, but the underlying profile is a mid-rotation righty who lets right-handed bats do damage. That's a problem in San Diego, because Tatis and Machado are the exact two hitters you don't want seeing a hard-hit rate north of 43% against your arm slot. Buehler isn't winning any Cy Young votes either, but the Padres are simply the better team by a wide margin, and Miami's lineup outside of Stowers doesn't punish command wobble the way San Diego's does. -134 on the roster edge plus the pitching matchup working quietly in your favor is the pitch.

Cleveland is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but Gavin Williams walks the ballpark and Jack Perkins has quietly been the sharper arm in this game all season. A run and a half is a lot of cushion when the projected margin is a couple of tenths and Williams is handing out free passes at a double-digit clip. Langeliers in particular gets the exact command-dependent righty profile he punishes, and the park is playing neutral enough that this stays a grinder. At -112 you're getting a coin flip on a game the market has already decided.

Griffin Jax is a strikeout monster against righties and a much more ordinary pitcher against everyone else, which matters when the Red Sox can roll out a lineup stacked with left-handed bats built to exploit exactly that split. Anthony, Abreu, and the rest don't need to win the game outright, they just need to keep it close, and Jax's numbers versus lefties (a .314 xwOBA that looks nothing like his overall line) suggest they will. Boston's own arm doesn't have to be brilliant either, because the sim sees a one-run game and the run line only asks them to lose by one.
